newsitem.title: UK: Sumitomo news hardly solves copper mystery.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo news hardly solves copper mystery.

text.p: Sumitomo Corp's announcment on Thursday of yet bigger losses from alleged rogue trades in copper lifted only a corner of the veil that shrouds its mysterious positions in the world metals market.
Copper prices were confounded by the news.
"This still leaves us a bit in the dark. It would be foolish to think that this marks the final chapter of the story," said Robin Bahr, an analyst with brokerage Brandeis in London.
Sumitomo said losses soared to $2.6 billion from $1.8 billion after it liquidated most of its uncovered positions.
But the statement by the huge Japanese metals house left the market in a quandary about whether more selling had to be done by banks that may have taken over Sumitomo's position.

Prices in London briefly popped higher on the news -- adding about $10 to $1,953 per tonne -- since traders had been fearing since Sumitomo first announced the losses in June that the firm would have to sell huge amounts of copper to unwind positions.
But by midday London Metal Exchange (LME) prices eased back to Wednesday's closing levels around $1,925.
Former star trader Yasuo Hamanaka, who may now face criminal charges, is thought to have piled up the copper in an effort to control prices.
"It's bullish on the face of it, since it removes some uncertainty, but I don't think we should get too carried away," Bahr said.
"Does it mean that Sumitomo has sold their book to somebody else and locked in a price?," analyst Jim Lennon of MacQuarie Equities said.
"There may well be some long positions run by some non-Sumitomo banks. Nobody knows and I think that dampened some of the initial euphoria," he added.
Sumitomo has been a massive force in the copper market, selling about 600,000 tonnes each year to customers, Bahr said.
The Sumitomo statement said all of its losses were made on the LME, the world's biggest forum for trading industrial metals where material is sold for future delivery.

Some analysts wondered why the firm failed to see losses from physical inventories, since many in the market had believed that Hamanaka kept huge stockpiles away from the market to keep prices artificially high.
"It all seems strange from what we thought the facts were...do they actually have physical stocks or do they have a position in the physical market that needs to be hedged on the LME?," Bahr asked.
Others said it was natural for a big trader like Sumitomo to hold stocks and doubted the stories about mysterious warehouses full of copper.
"The question is whether there was a significant hidden stockpile. I think the jury is out on that one, but the answer is tending to be no," said Lennon.
Prices have surged nearly $100 over the past few days and Thursday's news might give it some added momentum, analyst William Adams at broker Rudolf Wolff said.
"This might unnerve some shorts in the market," he said, adding that prices were soon likely to challenge a key level of $1,970.
In the long-term, however, projections of huge surpluses swamping the market would pressure prices.
"There's still a lot of uncertainty and nervousness in the market," Adams added.
